newsitem.title: UK: Callebaut plans chocolate school in Poland.
newsitem.headline: Callebaut plans chocolate school in Poland.

text.p: Chocolate maker and cocoa bean processor Barry Callebaut said it plans to open a chocolate college in Lodz, Poland this year to help lay the foundations for further chocolate consumption growth in that region.
"We're now also investing in a college in Poland," said Onno Bleeker, executive director of industrial sales and development. "Why? Because we want to educate people on how to use chocolate."
Barry Callebaut already has six schools worldwide in France, Belgium, Italy, the United States, Canada and Singapore.
The world's largest cocoa bean processor is also planning a larger, global Barry Callebaut Institute to improve cocoa and chocolate innovations, education and information worldwide.

The institute is expected to bring together an international research and development (R&D) centre federating the three existing R&D centres in North America, France and Belgium. It will also include an international communication centre providing information on cocoa and chocolate and an internaional training centre involving the chocolate colleges.
A spokeswoman said the first stage is expected to begin by the end of the year and the second phase in early 1998.
Moving developing markets beyond just buying and eating the finished chocolate bars by teaching them how to use chocolate and cocoa in other products is key to growing the market.

"It is not only (that) you are interested in big customers," Bleeker said. I think a market is built up by the smaller ones -- the bakeries, the pastry chefs, the small chocolatiers and then, gradually, the big industries will follow as well."
Because chocolate is seen as a luxury item people develop a taste for after incomes rise, many chocolate makers were hopeful for a new market after Eastern European communism collapsed.

Chocolate and cocoa consumption initially tumbled to very low levels immediately after communism fell, but chocolate makers and cocoa processors had expected economies there eventually to open up and people's living standards to rise to open the door to explosive growth.
Major chocolate manufacturers like Barry Callebaut, Cadbury Schweppes, Mars, Nestle and Kraft Jacobs Suchard have invested in production facilities in the region.

But though consumption has increased in the past two to three years, probably to about the levels seen before the fall of communism, the extent of that growth has remained more subdued and more unclear than in other emerging markets.

"Eastern Europe hasn't shown as much growth as in other areas" such as China and South America, an analyst said. But he did expect growth to continue, albeit at a slower pace compared to other developing regions.
Uncertainty in Eastern Europe was also reflected in Barry Callebaut's forecasts for world cocoa and chocolate consumption.

It forecasts a higher long-term trend for cocoa bean consumption in Western Europe, Eastern Europe, the Americas, Asia and Africa. That contrasts with expectations for about flat Eastern European growth.
For 1996/97, Callebaut estimated Eastern European cocoa bean consumption to fall to 158,000 tonnes from 1995/96's 163,000 tonnnes and 1994/95's 162,000 tonnes.
Barry Callebaut hopes to smooth out Eastern Europe's spotty growth by helping to grow the market through education on how to use chocolate and cocoa as ingredients in other foods.
"A chocolate college is quite vital for our existence and future existence because chocolate is a product that you can work with," Bleeker said.
